abstract: Leadership coaching develops managers but is expensive and difficult to scale. AI may be able to help scale access, but “answering machine” like AI coaching agents invite cognitive offloading and weaken learning. We instantiated a human coaching protocol, supported across prior cycles, as a text-based AI coach built to prompt reflective questioning. In the fourth cycle of a design-based research program at a global consulting firm, eight managers received the same protocol from a human coach and the AI coach, applied each session in an observed onboarding activity, and reflected on both in interviews. All eight welcomed the probing questions and preferred the human coach. Notably, they resisted the same protocol of questioning from the AI coach and wanted answers from it instead. This study’s theoretical contribution is the Reflection Penalty, the cost an AI coach pays for asking a user to do the reflective work that makes human coaching effective. Its practical contribution is a jobs-to-be-done map for AI coaching, assembled from proposals participants raised on their own. It divides coaching into distinct jobs and assigns each to the human or the AI best suited to it. Both contributions are offered to those designing AI tools that aim to support reflection

ur.tldr: 在全球咨询公司开展设计研究，8名管理者先后接受同一反思协议下的人类教练与AI文本教练辅导。结果显示尽管协议一致，管理者抗拒AI教练的发问式反思，期望其直接给答案。由此提出"反思惩罚"理论，并绘制人机协作的jobs-to-be-done地图，划分教练任务在人机间的分工。

title: The Reflection Penalty: when managers accept leadership coaching from a human but not an AI agent
title_zh: 反思惩罚：管理者接受人类而非AI代理领导力辅导的现象
